title: Safety in Practice: Hazard, Fire & Chemical Lab
subtitle: Hazard, fire and chemical lab
body_html:
MODULE 02 · SAFETY IN PRACTICE

This lab assumes you have completed module 01.
notes: Companion: Noor, char-noor-welcome, L1 half-body bottom-right (alt: Noor, the safety liaison, welcoming learners to the lab). Speaker: Noor. Brand D11 draft in use.
narration_text: Noor: Welcome to Safety in Practice: Hazard, Fire & Chemical Lab. You will practise decisions that help you act with confidence. You will leave with practical actions for your next shift.

title: The lab
body_html:
SECTION 1 OF 7 · SPOT THE HAZARD

Safety = the measures and practices that protect life, health and environment.

Today you practise, not read: spot hazards, run a Code Red drill, pick the right extinguisher, triage a spill and read a chemical register.
narration_text: Noor: Safety is the habits that protect life, health and environment. Today you practise them. Keep the main point connected to a familiar task or conversation. That connection makes the information easier to use when it matters. Use the principle in context. Keep the next action clear.

title: Teach risk scoring
intro_html: Problem: it is raining and the floor at the clinic entrance is wet. Score the risk as likelihood × impact (consequence), each on a 1–5 scale.

steps.action_html: Name the hazard: wet floor at a busy entrance.
steps.rationale_html: A hazard is something with the potential to cause harm to people, property or environment. Name it before you score it.
Likelihood asks how probable harm is. Many people cross a wet surface, so a slip is likely.
Impact asks how bad the harm would be. It is scored separately from likelihood because a rare event can still be severe.
Multiplying the two scores ranks this risk against others so you know what to fix first.

steps.action_html: Control: entrance mat + wet-floor sign + a mop schedule.
steps.rationale_html: Each control lowers a different part of the score: the mat and mopping cut likelihood; the sign warns people while the floor is still wet.

self_explanation_prompt_html: Why is the sign not enough on its own? This reflection is not scored.
narration_text: Noor: Walk through the wet-floor example aloud. Explain why likelihood and impact are scored separately. Follow the example one step at a time, then identify why the next step makes sense. The value is the reasoning you can carry into a similar case. Ask early when a situation does not match the rule. Good habits here are quiet: check, confirm, continue. Pause and connect this to your role. Use the principle in context. Keep the next action clear. Think of the first detail you would check. Apply the point to a familiar task. Carry the idea into your next decision.

title: Find the hazards
prompt_html:
Six hazards are hidden in this store room. Open all six markers to see the hazard and its control.

Noor's tip: “I walked past a blocked exit for a week before I noticed it.”
image_alt: Clinic store room: a staff member stands on a wheeled office chair reaching a high shelf, cables trail across the floor, boxes are stacked on top shelves and in front of the exit door, an unlabelled bottle sits on a shelf, and liquid has pooled under a wall socket.

regions.feedback_html: A chair with wheels can roll away and cause a fall from height. Control: use an approved step stool or kick step, and store heavy items lower.
Cables across a walkway are a trip hazard and get damaged underfoot. Control: reroute along the wall, use a cable cover, or report for a new socket.
Boxes in front of the exit and extinguisher slow everyone's escape and hide the equipment. Control: clear the exit now and keep the area marked and free at all times.
High stacks can fall and cause strain injuries when lifted down. Control: heavy items on low shelves, keep stacks below shoulder height.
Nobody can tell what is inside, what it does or how to clean it up. Control: do not use it; label it from the register and SDS, or remove it through EHS.
Liquid next to electricity is a shock and slip hazard. Control: keep people away, do not touch the plug with wet hands, report it and clean the spill safely.

feedback.correct_html: All six found. Next, decide which one to fix first.
feedback.incorrect_html: Open the remaining markers to find all six hazards.

notes: Companion: Noor, char-noor-avatar-neutral + tip card, L3 tip card bottom-left (blocked-exit story, companions.md §1); tip text is in prompt_html. Hotspot coordinates measured on hs2-img-storeroom.png (1672 × 941 px). The Safety Manager must still confirm the six-hazard answer key (B6).
narration_text: Noor: Set up the store room. There are six hazards. Open them all. I walked past a blocked exit for a week before I noticed it. Let each marker add context rather than rushing to a conclusion.

title: Prioritise
prompt_html: You found six hazards in the store room. Which one do you report and fix first?

options.text_html: The boxes blocking the fire exit and extinguisher
options.feedback_html: Right. A blocked exit has a severe impact on everyone in the building if a fire starts, so it ranks highest.
A real trip hazard with a high likelihood, but the impact is usually one person's fall. The blocked exit could affect everyone.

options.text_html: The unlabelled bottle on the shelf
options.feedback_html: Important to fix, but the likelihood of harm right now is low while nobody uses it. A blocked exit affects everyone in an emergency.

options.text_html: The person standing on the wheeled chair
options.feedback_html: Stop them, yes, but that's one person and one moment. The blocked exit is a standing risk for the whole building.

feedback.correct_html: Compare likelihood and impact: the blocked exit has the highest impact for the most people.
feedback.incorrect_html: Compare impact as well as likelihood: which hazard could harm the most people at once?

narration_text: Noor: The next choice asks you to apply the rule in a workplace situation. Read carefully, then choose.

title: Score a risk

feedback.correct_html: Right: 2 × 5 = 10. Low likelihood, but severe harm still needs a control.
feedback.incorrect_html: Multiply likelihood by impact: 2 × 5. Low likelihood, but severe harm still needs a control.

title: Code Red drill
intro_html:
Code Red drill. A weekday afternoon in the clinic. Smoke is coming from Consultation Room 3 on the first floor.

Six decisions, one for each moment of the response. You have 2 lives and one text hint per decision. There is no timer here, but in real life seconds matter. Pass: at least 5 of 6 right.

Code wording and extension ⚠ Draft — pending D2. Assembly-point names ⚠ Draft — pending B8.

hints.text: Decision 1 · Rescue: who is in immediate danger right now?
Decision 2 · Alarm: the call has three parts — code type, location, your ID and name.
Decision 3 · Contain: what would feed the fire, and what stops the smoke spreading?
Decision 4 · Extinguish: two conditions must both be true — the fire is small and you are trained.
Decision 5 · Evacuate: which evacuation tool is made for stairs?
Decision 6 · Assembly: who decides when it is safe to go back inside?

nodes.image_alt: Consultation room with smoke building near the ceiling and an unnamed patient still in the chair.
nodes.content_html: 1 · Rescue. You open the door of Consultation Room 3. Smoke is gathering under the ceiling and the patient is still in the chair. What do you do first?

choices.text_html: Help the patient out of the room to a safe place, then raise the alarm.
choices.feedback_html: Right. R — Rescue: anyone in immediate danger comes first. The alarm follows straight after.

choices.text_html: Go to the nursing-station phone and call first.
choices.feedback_html: Poster rule: RACE starts with Rescue — move anyone in immediate danger before you go to the phone. The patient was left in a smoke-filled room. You lose a life.

choices.text_html: Look for where the smoke is coming from before doing anything else.
choices.feedback_html: Poster rule: Rescue first. Investigating the source while a patient breathes smoke wastes the seconds that matter. You lose a life.

nodes.image_alt: Fire alarm call point on a corridor wall beside a telephone.
nodes.content_html:
2 · Alarm. The patient is safe in the corridor. You shout “Code Red!” and pull the call point. Dr. Omar comes out of the next room: “I'll call it in. What exactly do I say?”

He dials the clinic emergency extension (⚠ Draft — pending D2). Which script is complete?

choices.text_html: “Code Red, Consultation Room 3, first floor. This is Dr. Omar, staff ID 4417.”
choices.feedback_html: Right. A — Alarm: shout “Code Red”, activate the call point, then call and state the code type, location, and your ID and name. All three are here.

choices.text_html: “There's a fire, please come quickly!”
choices.feedback_html: Poster rule: the call must give the code type, location, and your ID and name. This script gives none of them, so the team doesn't know where to go. You lose a life.

choices.text_html: “Code Red on the first floor.”
choices.feedback_html: Poster rule: code type, exact location, ID and name. “First floor” is not a location the team can go straight to, and nobody knows who called. You lose a life.

nodes.image_alt: Consultation room with an oxygen cylinder, a wall-mounted alcohol rub dispenser, a patient file on the desk and the door.
nodes.content_html: 3 · Contain. The room has an oxygen cylinder, an alcohol rub dispenser and the patient's paper file. What do you do before you leave?

choices.text_html: Remove the O₂ cylinder and the alcohol rub, then close the door.
choices.feedback_html: Right. C — Contain: remove oxygen cylinders and alcohol-based sanitiser, which feed a fire, and close the room's door to hold back smoke.

choices.text_html: Remove the O₂ cylinder, the alcohol rub and the patient file, and leave the door open so you can watch the fire.
choices.feedback_html: Poster rule: close the room's doors. An open door lets smoke and fire spread down the corridor. The file is not a fire hazard to remove. You lose a life.

choices.text_html: Take the patient file to protect the record, then close the door.
choices.feedback_html: Poster rule: remove the oxygen cylinders and alcohol rub — they feed the fire. The file can wait; the oxygen can't. You lose a life.

nodes.image_alt: Two states of the same room: a small fire inside a metal waste bin, and flames spreading up a curtain into the ceiling.
nodes.content_html: 4 · Extinguish or evacuate? The picture shows two ways this could look: a small fire inside the metal waste bin, or flames climbing the curtain into the ceiling. Which rule do you follow?

choices.text_html: If it is a small bin fire and I am trained, use the extinguisher (PASS) with my exit behind me. If it is spreading, evacuate.
choices.feedback_html: Right. E — Extinguish / Evacuate: extinguish small fires only if you are trained to do so. A spreading fire means you leave and evacuate.

choices.text_html: Always try to put it out first, even if it is spreading. Evacuation is the last resort.
choices.feedback_html: Poster rule: extinguish small fires only, and only if trained. A spreading fire is an evacuation. You lose a life.

choices.text_html: Anyone can use an extinguisher, so fight it whether you are trained or not.
choices.feedback_html: Poster rule: extinguish small fires if trained to do so. Untrained use wastes time and puts you at risk. You lose a life.

nodes.image_alt: Generic stairwell with an evacuation chair and an unnamed wheelchair user waiting with a staff member.
nodes.content_html: 5 · Evacuate. Evacuation is called. A patient who uses a wheelchair and cannot walk is on the first floor. How do you get them down?

choices.text_html: Transfer them to the evacuation chair and take the stairs with a trained colleague.
choices.feedback_html: Right. Rescue patients using evacuation tools: the evacuation chair is made for stairs.

choices.text_html: Take the elevator. It's faster for a wheelchair.
choices.feedback_html: Poster rule: use the evacuation tools — the evacuation chair on the stairs. Elevators can stop or open onto the fire floor during a fire. You lose a life.

choices.text_html: Leave them in the room and tell the fire team where they are.
choices.feedback_html: Poster rule: rescue patients using evacuation tools. An evacuation chair lets two trained staff bring them down the stairs now. You lose a life.

nodes.image_alt: Generic outdoor assembly point with unnamed colleagues and patients waiting.
nodes.content_html: 6 · Assembly point. You reach the outside assembly point (⚠ Draft — pending B8) with the patient. The smoke seems to have cleared and some colleagues start walking back in. What do you do?

choices.text_html: Stay, report to the person in charge, and wait for the all-clear (“End of disaster”) before anyone goes back.
choices.feedback_html: Right. Nobody re-enters until the End of disaster announcement. Reporting in means the team can account for everyone. Announcement wording ⚠ Draft — pending D2.

choices.text_html: Go back in to fetch your bag now that the smoke has cleared.
choices.feedback_html: Rule: wait for the all-clear. Smoke clearing doesn't mean the building is safe, and the team needs to count everyone at the assembly point. You lose a life.

choices.text_html: Go home. Your part is done.
choices.feedback_html: Rule: stay at the assembly point until the all-clear. If you leave, the team may think you are still inside and search for you. You lose a life.

nodes.content_html:
Drill debrief — RACE

  1. Rescue — the patient out of the smoke first.
  2. Alarm — shout “Code Red”, pull the call point, call: code type, location, ID and name.
  3. Contain — remove O₂ and alcohol rub, close the door.
  4. Extinguish — only a small fire, only if trained (PASS); otherwise evacuate.
  5. Evacuate — evacuation chair on the stairs, never the elevator.
  6. Assembly point — report in and wait for the all-clear.

choices.text_html: Finish the drill and see your score.
choices.feedback_html: Drill complete. Check your score below.

feedback.correct_html: Drill passed. You followed Rescue → Alarm → Contain → Extinguish or Evacuate, and waited for the all-clear.
feedback.incorrect_html: Drill not passed. RACE debrief: Rescue the person in danger · Alarm: “Code Red”, call point, then code type + location + ID and name · Contain: remove O₂ and alcohol rub, close the door · Extinguish a small fire only if trained, otherwise Evacuate (evacuation chair on stairs) · wait at the assembly point for the all-clear. Revisit this screen to run the drill again.

notes: Companions: char-noor-avatar-neutral hosts the drill as the L5 avatar on the intro; char-omar-avatar-neutral is the colleague making the alarm call in node 2 (named in the node text; the game schema has no per-node avatar slot). (Phase 3 table: Noor avatar as host; Omar avatar in node 2.) Six scenes hs2-img-drill-1..6, one per node (G10 full six-scene drill); all gated on Safety Manager sign-off of nodes, code wording and assembly-point treatment. Score +1 per correct RACE choice (multiplier off), 2 lives, pass 5 of 6, no timer. Hints are one ladder of six text hints in node order (engine reveals them in sequence). Open decisions shown as drafts: D2 (code wording, extension, End-of-disaster wording), B8 (assembly-point names). Staff ID 4417 is fictional.
narration_text: Noor: The next choice asks you to apply the rule in a workplace situation. Read carefully, then choose. Use the rule you practised. Focus on the action that fits. Feedback explains the reasoning after you respond. Dr. Omar: Carry this practical rule into your next decision.

title: Tool ↔ patient
prompt_html: Match each patient to the evacuation tool you would use.

items.text_html: Adult who can't walk, stairs needed
Infant carried by a staff member

feedback.correct_html: Right. Mattress for a bedbound adult, chair for stairs, newborn evacuation chair for the nursery, baby mover or apron when staff carry infants.
feedback.incorrect_html: Match the tool to how the patient moves: lying down → mattress; seated on stairs → evacuation chair; newborns → newborn evacuation chair; carried infants → baby mover / apron.

narration_text: Noor: The next choice asks you to apply the rule in a workplace situation. Read carefully, then choose.

title: A plan
prompt_html:
This is a generic practice plan, not a real floor plan. Read its legend, then give each numbered marker its label.

  • The arrow leaving “You are here” is the way out.
  • Zone B: the call point, on the corridor wall.
  • Zone C: the fire extinguisher.
  • Zone D: the fire hose reel cabinet.
  • Zone E: the staff kitchen, with the fire blanket.
  • Outside the building, beyond Zone D: the assembly point.
image_alt: Generic evacuation floor plan with zones A to E, a 'You are here' marker in zone A and an arrow showing the way out.

feedback.correct_html: Right. You read the legend and matched each symbol to its place. Find your own unit's plan on the wall today and do the same.
feedback.incorrect_html: Check the legend again: match each marker's zone to the item listed for that zone, and remember the assembly point is outside the building.

notes: hs2-img-floorplan.svg currently has zones and 'You are here' only; the Phase 3 brief also asks for legend icons. Marker positions (0–1000) assume the legend is added at these spots; re-check positions when the SVG is revised. Real floor plans are never packaged (B7).
narration_text: Noor: The next choice asks you to apply the rule in a workplace situation. Read carefully, then choose.

title: Assembly points

blocks.html:
Two assembly points

Inside assembly point: a safe area inside the building, used in horizontal or vertical evacuation.

Outside assembly point: the signed meeting place outside, used in a full evacuation. Names per branch ⚠ Draft — pending B8.

Three levels of evacuation (recap from module 01)

Horizontal (to the next safe zone on the same floor) → vertical (down to a lower floor) → full (out of the building).
Find your unit's evacuation plan on the wall today.

narration_text: Noor: Inside vs outside assembly points. Find your unit's plan today. As you read, focus on the decision this information supports in your own role. The aim is a practical next action, not a phrase to memorise. If one detail stays with you, let it be the safe one. Ask early when a situation does not match the rule.

title: The label
prompt_html: Before you ever need it, know how to read the extinguisher. Open all five parts to see what to check.
image_alt: My Clinic dry-powder fire extinguisher with its safety pin, pressure gauge, class label, instructions panel and inspection tag.

regions.feedback_html: Check the pin and its tamper seal are in place. A missing seal can mean it has been used.
The needle must be in the green. Outside the green, report it: it may not work.
Read the agent (here dry powder, ABC) and the fire classes it is rated for before you use it.
Pull the pin · Aim at the base of the fire · Squeeze the handle · Sweep side to side.
Check the date of the last inspection. An overdue tag means you report it to Safety & Security.

feedback.correct_html: All five checked: pin, gauge, label, PASS and inspection tag.
feedback.incorrect_html: Open the remaining parts of the extinguisher.

notes: hs2-img-extinguisher is a planned client photo (permission + EHS equipment review pending). Region coordinates are placeholders on the 960 × 540 pending card and must be re-measured on the final 3:4 photo.
narration_text: Noor: Before you need it, know how to read the label and check the gauge. Explore the marked areas at your own pace, then compare the details you found. Use those details to identify the next practical action. Apply the point to a familiar task.

title: Match the fire
prompt_html: Match each fire to the extinguisher you would use.

items.text_html: Pan of oil in the staff kitchen

feedback.correct_html: Right. Electrical equipment (class C) → CO₂ · cooking oils and fats (class K) → wet chemical · ordinary solids like cardboard (class A) → water or ABC powder · flammable liquids (class B) → foam.
feedback.incorrect_html: Match the agent to the class: A ordinary solids → water / ABC powder; B flammable liquids → foam; C electrical → CO₂ (never water); K cooking oil → wet chemical.

narration_text: Noor: The next choice asks you to apply the rule in a workplace situation. Read carefully, then choose.

title: What is HAZMAT; Code Orange

blocks.html: HAZMAT — any substance or agent that, if released or misused, can pose a threat to the environment, life or health.
Code Orange — a leak or release of hazardous material: a chemical or a biological spill.

One rule decides Code Orange: Spill of 500 mL or more, or any highly toxic, reactive or explosive substance → Code Orange. Otherwise call the cleaning supervisor's trained team.

⚠ Draft — pending D1: the source deck gives two thresholds (under 1 L “minor” and over 500 mL); this is the recommended single rule.

notes: Code Orange threshold uses the decision sheet's recommended draft for D1 (02/B1). Change the rule text here, in hs2-052 and in hs2-064 puzzle 4 when D1 closes.
narration_text: Noor: HAZMAT is chemical or biological. One clear rule decides Code Orange. Notice which part of the information you would need first in practice. Use that as the starting point for a safe, respectful next action. Keep the next action clear. Think of the first detail you would check. Apply the point to a familiar task.

title: Two kits
prompt_html: Two kits, two colours, two jobs. Drag the divider to compare them.
caption: A spill kit is equipment designed to remove hazardous substances quickly and efficiently. Red kit: for chemical spills. Yellow kit with the biohazard symbol: for blood and body fluids. Contents lists of each kit come from EHS ⚠ Draft — pending B4.
notes: Both photos are planned client photos (same angle and size; permission and EHS equipment review pending). Alt text: 'Red chemical spill kit.' / 'Yellow biological spill kit.' (image_compare has no alt fields; labels carry the meaning). Kit contents pending B4.
narration_text: Noor: Two kits, two colours, two jobs. Compare the two views carefully and look for the detail that changes the decision or next action. The contrast is there to make the practical signal easier to spot.

title: Spill triage
intro_html:
Three spills on one shift. For each, decide the kit and whether to call Code Orange.

The rule: Spill of 500 mL or more, or any highly toxic, reactive or explosive substance → Code Orange. Otherwise call the cleaning supervisor's trained team. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

nodes.prompt_html: A urine sample pot is dropped in the lab corridor and splashes on the floor.

choices.text_html: Isolate the area and clean it with the biological spill kit. No Code Orange.
choices.feedback_html: Right. A small biological spill, nothing highly toxic: below the threshold, so no Code Orange. Use the yellow biological kit. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

choices.text_html: Call Code Orange: any body fluid is hazardous material.
choices.feedback_html: The rule: Code Orange at 500 mL or more, or a highly toxic, reactive or explosive substance. One sample is neither. Use the biological kit. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

choices.text_html: Wipe it up with paper towels and carry on.
choices.feedback_html: No Code Orange is needed, but body fluids still need the biological kit and PPE, not bare paper towels.

nodes.prompt_html: A one-litre container of surface disinfectant tips over in the store. Most of it is on the floor.

choices.text_html: Call Code Orange.
choices.feedback_html: Right. Well over 500 mL of a chemical is above the threshold: Code Orange. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

choices.text_html: Clean it yourself with the chemical spill kit. It's only disinfectant.
choices.feedback_html: The rule is about volume as well as toxicity: 500 mL or more means Code Orange, whatever the product. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

choices.text_html: Call the cleaning supervisor and leave it for the next shift.
choices.feedback_html: The cleaning supervisor handles spills below the threshold. This one is above 500 mL: Code Orange, and nobody leaves it. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

nodes.prompt_html: A few drops of a reagent labelled “highly toxic” leak from a cracked vial in the lab.

choices.text_html: Call Code Orange, even though the volume is tiny.
choices.feedback_html: Right. Any highly toxic, reactive or explosive substance means Code Orange, regardless of volume. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

choices.text_html: It's only a few drops, so clean it with the chemical spill kit.
choices.feedback_html: Volume isn't the only test: any highly toxic substance means Code Orange. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

choices.text_html: Use the biological spill kit.
choices.feedback_html: This is a chemical, and a highly toxic one: Code Orange, regardless of volume. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

feedback.correct_html: Three for three. One rule: Spill of 500 mL or more, or any highly toxic, reactive or explosive substance → Code Orange. Otherwise call the cleaning supervisor's trained team.
feedback.incorrect_html: Check each spill against the single rule: Spill of 500 mL or more, or any highly toxic, reactive or explosive substance → Code Orange. Otherwise call the cleaning supervisor's trained team.

notes: Companion: Dr. Omar hosts — char-omar-avatar-neutral on the intro (L5), char-omar-avatar-happy / char-omar-avatar-concern after choices. Rule text is the D1 recommended draft (pending D1).
narration_text: Noor: The next choice asks you to apply the rule in a workplace situation. Read carefully, then choose.

title: Spill-kit procedure
prompt_html: Put the chemical spill-kit procedure in order. Procedure ⚠ Draft — pending B4 (EHS writes the final steps).

items.text_html: Put on PPE as the SDS requires
Isolate the area and warn others
Contain the edges of the spill
Bag, seal and label as hazardous waste
Clean the area and report to your supervisor and Safety Services

feedback.correct_html: Right. Protect yourself, protect others, stop it spreading, remove it, dispose of it safely, report, and leave the kit ready for the next person.
feedback.incorrect_html: Think from the outside in: PPE before you touch anything, warn people, stop the spread at the edges, then absorb, bag, report and restock.

notes: Seven steps from the Phase 2 card (B4 proposed procedure; source p.29 is blank). Pending B4.
narration_text: Noor: The next choice asks you to apply the rule in a workplace situation. Read carefully, then choose.

title: How to read a register

blocks.html: Read a register row left to right: what it is, its hazard class, why it's here, how much, is the SDS on file, and what the NFPA diamond says.

#ProductHazard classPurposeQtySDSNFPA H-F-R-S
1Alcohol-based hand rubFlammableHand hygiene1.3 L✓per SDS
2Foaming hand soapIrritantHand washing1.3 L✓per SDS
3Solvent (isopropyl alcohol 70%)FlammableDisinfection250 mL✓2-3-0 · —

SDS column: ✓ means the Safety Data Sheet is on file. ✘ means do not use the product until the SDS is supplied: report it to your supervisor or EHS.

narration_text: Noor: Read a register row left to right: what it is, why it's here, is the SDS on file, what the diamond says. As you read, focus on the decision this information supports in your own role. The aim is a practical next action, not a phrase to memorise. Pause and connect this to your role. Use the principle in context. Keep the next action clear. Think of the first detail you would check. Apply the point to a familiar task.

title: GHS hazard statements
prompt_html: Match each GHS pictogram to an example of the hazard it warns about.

pairs.right_html: Skin burns, eye damage, corrosive to metals
Flammable liquids, pyrophorics, emits flammable gas
Irritant to skin and eyes, skin sensitiser, narcotic effects

feedback.correct_html: Right. Nine pictograms, nine hazards. Read the pictogram before you open the bottle.
feedback.incorrect_html: Watch the look-alikes: the plain flame means flammable; the flame over a circle means an oxidiser that feeds a fire. The exclamation mark is irritant or harmful; the health-hazard figure is long-term harm.

notes: Pictograms are named as text: the matching schema has no image slot, so planned <hs2-img-ghs-1..9> (reuse of module 01 GHS SVGs) cannot be placed on this screen type.

title: Register decision
prompt_html:
Register row 4: Surface disinfectant X — SDS ✘.

You need it for a cleaning task right now. What do you do?

options.text_html: Don't use it. Report the missing SDS to your supervisor or EHS.
options.feedback_html: Right. Without the SDS nobody can confirm the hazards, the PPE or the spill response. Use another product with an SDS on file.

options.text_html: Use it carefully. The label on the bottle is enough.
options.feedback_html: The label is a summary. The SDS tells you the PPE, first aid and spill response. No SDS, no use.

options.text_html: Use it with gloves, then report the missing SDS afterwards.
options.feedback_html: Gloves may not be the right PPE, and you can't know without the SDS. Report first, and don't use it until the SDS is on file.

options.text_html: Find any SDS for a similar product online and go ahead.
options.feedback_html: A similar product's SDS may not match this one. The register needs the SDS for this exact product.

feedback.correct_html: No SDS, no use: report it to your supervisor or EHS.
feedback.incorrect_html: Look at the SDS column: ✘ means don't use it until the SDS is on file.

narration_text: Noor: The next choice asks you to apply the rule in a workplace situation. Read carefully, then choose.

title: NFPA in practice
prompt_html:
Register row 3: Solvent (isopropyl alcohol 70%), NFPA 2-3-0 (health 2 · flammability 3 · reactivity 0).

Where must it be stored?

options.text_html: In an approved flammable-storage cabinet, away from heat
options.feedback_html: Right. Flammability 3 means it ignites easily at normal temperatures, so it belongs in the self-closing flammable cabinet, away from heat and ignition sources.

options.text_html: On an open shelf, as long as it is labelled
options.feedback_html: A label doesn't stop vapour reaching a heat source. Flammability 3 needs the flammable cabinet.

options.text_html: In the staff fridge to keep it cool
options.feedback_html: A domestic fridge has ignition sources inside and is never for chemicals. Use the flammable cabinet.

options.text_html: Under the sink with the cleaning products
options.feedback_html: Mixed storage and no fire protection. Flammability 3 means the approved flammable cabinet.

feedback.incorrect_html: Read the red (flammability) number first: 3 means it ignites easily.

notes: Diamond given as text in the prompt. The planned SVG hs2-img-nfpa-230 cannot be placed on an mcq, and the current SVG places 2 on the yellow and 3 on the red quadrant with 0 outside the diamond and the standard quadrant positions swapped; fix the asset before any reuse.

puzzles.prompt_html:
NFPA diamond on the solvent (row 3): blue / health 2 · red / flammability 3 · yellow / reactivity 0 · white / special: blank.

What is the solvent's health rating?
Which register row has no SDS on file? Enter the row number.
puzzles.hint_html: Look down the SDS column for a ✘.

puzzles.prompt_html: A colleague is splashed in the eye. For at least how many minutes do you flush at the eyewash station?
puzzles.hint_html: Longer than feels comfortable: a quarter of an hour (module 01 eyewash rule).

puzzles.prompt_html:
In the store, a one-litre bottle of disinfectant lies on its side, more than half of it on the floor. Which code do you call?

Rule: Spill of 500 mL or more, or any highly toxic, reactive or explosive substance → Code Orange. Otherwise call the cleaning supervisor's trained team. ⚠ Draft — pending D1
puzzles.hint_html: Check the volume against the 500 mL threshold.

feedback.correct_html: Door open. Debrief: (1) 2 — health is the blue quadrant of the NFPA diamond on the label. (2) Row 4 — the SDS column of your department's register. (3) 15 minutes — the sign at every eyewash station. (4) Code Orange — more than 500 mL spilled (⚠ Draft — pending D1). At work, all four answers are on the register, the label and the wall.
feedback.incorrect_html: The door stays locked. Debrief: health rating = blue quadrant (2); missing SDS = the ✘ in the register (row 4); eyewash = at least 15 minutes; over 500 mL spilled = Code Orange (⚠ Draft — pending D1). Revisit this screen to try again.

Puzzle 4 follows the D1 recommended draft (pending D1). Register rows pending B5. Eyewash 15 minutes is a module 01 fact (01 p.39).

title: Allowed or prohibited?
prompt_html:
Allowed or prohibited in the clinic? Sort each item.

Items marked approved are draft examples until the Safety Manager confirms the approved list (Phase 0 §3).

feedback.correct_html: Right. Candles, heaters, unauthorised extensions, smoking or vaping, and overheating food are all ignition or overload risks. Approved, tagged equipment in its approved place is allowed.
feedback.incorrect_html: Ask what could start a fire: an open flame, a heater, an untested home extension, vaping, or food left in the microwave too long. Items approved by Facilities or tagged by BME are allowed.

title: Per-objective results
body_html: Passing score: 80% (116 / 145 points). Any objective below 70% shows what to revisit.

sections.title: hs2-o1 · Spot hazards and score risk
sections.advice_html: Revisit the wet-floor example and the store room: likelihood × impact, then fix the highest risk first.

sections.title: hs2-o2 · Code Red drill (RACE)
sections.advice_html: Run the Code Red drill again: Rescue, Alarm (code type + location + ID and name), Contain, Extinguish or Evacuate.

sections.title: hs2-o3 · Evacuation tools and plans
sections.advice_html: Review the four evacuation tools and the floor-plan legend, then find your unit's plan.

sections.title: hs2-o4 · Extinguishers
sections.advice_html: Review the extinguisher label and the fire classes A, B, C and K.

sections.title: hs2-o5 · Spills
sections.advice_html: Review the Code Orange rule and the spill-kit procedure.

sections.title: hs2-o6 · GHS, NFPA and the register
sections.advice_html: Review how to read a register row, the GHS pictograms and the NFPA diamond.

sections.title: hs2-o7 · Prohibited items
sections.advice_html: Review the prohibited-items list and why each one is a fire risk.

narration_text: Noor: Your results are organised by objective. Notice where you were confident, then revisit any section that needs another practical try. Use that insight to choose what to revisit.

title: Close
body_html:
What you practised

  • Spot hazards and score risk as likelihood × impact.
  • Run RACE in a Code Red, with a complete alarm call.
  • Choose evacuation tools and extinguishers, and read a plan.
  • Triage spills, use the right kit, and read GHS, NFPA and the chemical register.
